themes.theme: Funding and staffing of supervisors and enforcers
themes.definition: Provisions that give the bodies which supervise and enforce the AI rules money, staff, technical means and infrastructure, or that say who pays for that work.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act (EU046, Art. 70(3)) requires Member States to ensure that their national competent authorities have 'adequate' technical, financial and human resources and infrastructure; the coder note adds that staff must have competences including an in-depth understanding of AI technologies, data and data computing, and personal data protection. At EU level the AI Act (Art. 64(1)) says only that the Commission shall develop Union expertise and capabilities through the AI Office; the Omnibus amendments (EU_Omnibus) add a new Art. 64(3) that the AI Office 'shall be allocated adequate resources', written in the passive and qualified 'without prejudice to the budgetary procedure' (the coder note says its recital 29 names the Commission as the one who should allocate them). The Omnibus also authorises the AI Office to reclaim from the operator concerned the full cost of supervising and enforcing a case of non-compliance, including staff and technical costs, and sets the fee Member States may have to pay for advice from the scientific panel. No passage gives a figure, a staffing level or a test of what counts as 'adequate'. [inference] The Omnibus moves part of the cost of enforcement onto operators found non-compliant, and part of the cost of expert support onto Member States, rather than funding both centrally.
themes.holders: Member States (for their national competent authorities); the Commission, through the AI Office; the Omnibus article on AI Office resources names no holder (passive voice); the 'relevant operator' pays reclaimed costs; Member States pay fees for expert advice.
themes.binding: Statutory: 'shall ensure' (Member States) and 'shall develop' (Commission). The Omnibus 'shall be allocated' is passive and subject to the budgetary procedure. Cost recovery is a statutory power ('shall be authorised to fully reclaim'); fees are a possibility ('may be required to pay'). No consequence is stated if resources are not adequate.

quotes.quote: Member States shall ensure that their national competent authorities are provided with adequate technical, financial and human resources, and with infrastructure to fulfil their tasks effectively under this Regulation.
The Commission shall develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office.

quotes.location: Art. 1(27), adding AI Act Art. 64(3); p. 26
quotes.quote: Without prejudice to the budgetary procedure, the AI Office shall be allocated adequate resources to effectively perform its duties and exercise its powers in relation to the enforcement of this Regulation.

quotes.location: Art. 1(32), inserting AI Act Art. 75a(1); p. 28
quotes.quote: The AI Office shall be authorised to fully reclaim from the relevant operator the totality of the costs of its supervision and enforcement activities with respect to instances of non-compliance, including costs for human and technical resources

themes.definition: A pool of independent experts, set up by the Commission, on which the AI Office, market surveillance authorities and Member States can draw for enforcement and for building tools to evaluate AI models.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires the Commission to make provisions for a scientific panel of independent experts 'intended to support the enforcement activities' of the Regulation (Art. 68(1)); the recital frames it mainly around the AI Office's monitoring of general-purpose AI models (Recital 151). According to the coder notes, experts are chosen by the Commission for up-to-date scientific or technical expertise and must be independent of any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models. The panel's listed tasks include contributing to tools and methodologies for evaluating the capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems, 'including through benchmarks', and supporting market surveillance authorities at their request. Member States 'may call upon' the experts for their own enforcement, with the Commission to facilitate access (the coder note is cut off at this point), and the recital presents this as a way to reinforce national capacities. The Omnibus amendments set the fee Member States may be required to pay, at a rate equivalent to the remuneration fees applicable to the Commission, so national use of the panel may carry a direct cost.
themes.holders: The Commission (sets up the panel, selects experts, facilitates access); the scientific panel (provides support); recipients are the AI Office, market surveillance authorities and Member States.
themes.binding: Setting up the panel is a statutory duty on the Commission (Art. 68(1)). Use is optional and on request ('may call upon', 'at their request'); the recitals use 'should'. Fees 'may' be required. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: The panel contributes to tools and methodologies for evaluating the capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems. Trigger: not stated. Compared against: 'benchmarks', none named. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the panel contributes; the coder note says the tools serve the AI Office's supervision of general-purpose models. What happens with the result: not stated. No passage concerns checking the outputs of an AI tool used by a public body.

quotes.quote: make provisions on the establishment of a scientific panel of independent experts (the ‘scientific panel’) intended to support the enforcement activities under this Regulation
contributing to the development of tools and methodologies for evaluating capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems, including through benchmarks
Member States may call upon experts of the scientific panel to support their enforcement activities under this Regulation.

quotes.location: Art. 1(28), replacing AI Act Art. 69(2); p. 26
quotes.quote: The Member States may be required to pay fees for the advice and support provided by the experts at a rate equivalent to the remuneration fees applicable to the Commission

themes.theme: Testing structures and appointed outside evaluators and auditors
themes.definition: Structures and powers through which the Commission, the AI Office and national authorities can bring in independent testers, evaluators, experts and auditors to examine AI systems and models.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act provides for 'Union AI testing support structures', which the recital says should be established and made available to Member States (Recital 152, which does not say who establishes them) and which the article says shall give independent technical or scientific advice when the Board, the Commission or market surveillance authorities ask (Art. 84(2)); the coder note says the Commission designates them. For general-purpose AI models, the Commission may appoint independent experts, including from the scientific panel, to carry out evaluations on its behalf (Art. 92(2)); the recital says the same of the AI Office (Recital 164). The Omnibus amendments widen this for monitoring compliance (new Art. 75a(7)): the AI Office may appoint independent external experts and auditors and, with the agreement of the authority concerned, experts, investigative teams and auditors from Member States' competent authorities. The passages say who may be brought in, not how testing or evaluation is to be done. [inference] These resources are aimed at examining providers' systems and models for market surveillance and enforcement; none is directed at a public body checking the AI tools it uses.
themes.holders: The Commission and the AI Office (appoint or designate); Union AI testing support structures; independent experts and external auditors (outside the state, per coder inference on 016); experts, investigative teams and auditors from Member States' competent authorities.
themes.binding: Mostly powers: 'may decide to appoint', 'may appoint', and the recital 'should be able to'. The testing structures' advice is a statutory 'shall provide', but only on request. Recital 152 says the structures 'should be established'. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: a request from the Board, the Commission or a market surveillance authority (testing support structures); a Commission or AI Office decision to evaluate (independent experts). What prompts an evaluation is not stated in these passages. Compared against: not stated (the scientific panel is to help develop benchmarks, EU-ACC-RES-024, none named). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: independent experts, testing support structures, external auditors or national authority staff, acting for the Commission or AI Office. What happens with the result: not stated; because evaluations are carried out 'on its behalf', results go to the Commission or AI Office [inference].

quotes.quote: Union AI testing support structures shall also provide independent technical or scientific advice at the request of the Board, the Commission, or of market surveillance authorities.
The Commission may decide to appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, including from the scientific panel established pursuant to Article 68.

quotes.location: Art. 1(32), inserting AI Act Art. 75a(7); p. 30
quotes.quote: the AI Office may appoint independent external experts and auditors, as well as experts, investigative teams and auditors from the Member State’s competent authorities with the agreement of the authority concerned.

themes.theme: Access to information, documentation, data and systems for overseers
themes.definition: Powers and arrangements that give supervisors and other oversight bodies access to the documentation, data, information or technical means they need to hold providers and deployers to account.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to give market surveillance authorities access 'where appropriate and subject to security safeguards' through application programming interfaces or other means of remote access (Art. 74(12)); the quote is a fragment that does not name what is accessed, and the coder note describes it as access tools for supervisors. Recitals add that market surveillance authorities should be able to obtain all personal data being processed and all information needed for their tasks (Recital 159), that national public authorities supervising fundamental-rights obligations should have access to any documentation created under the Regulation where their mandate needs it (Recital 157), and that the scientific panel should be able to ask the Commission to require documentation from a provider (Recital 163). The Omnibus amendments (new Art. 77(1a)) route fundamental-rights bodies' access through the market surveillance authority, which 'shall grant' it, if need be by requesting the material from the provider or deployer, 'where necessary and without undue delay' (coder note). The Commission guidelines (EU043) say providers and deployers should be able to explain how the system works and what types of data and data sources it uses when checked, and refer to the AI Act and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 for the authorities' enforcement powers without listing them. Under the Code of Practice (EU121), a signatory provider that stops a detection solution without replacing it will hand it to market surveillance authorities so they can still detect legacy content.
themes.holders: Market surveillance authorities; national public authorities or bodies supervising fundamental rights; the scientific panel (through the Commission); providers and deployers (who must supply access or information); signatory providers under the Code (detection tools).
themes.binding: Art. 74(12) is a statutory duty on providers; the Omnibus Art. 77(1a) is a statutory duty on market surveillance authorities; Recitals 157, 159 and 163 use 'should'; EU043 is non-binding interpretation; the Code commitment ('will') binds signatories only. What follows if access is refused is not stated in these passages.
themes.checks: Remote access through APIs (EU-ACC-RES-004) is a means by which supervisors can examine a high-risk system [inference]; trigger, comparison, metric, who and outcome are not stated. Detection tools handed over under the Code (EU-ACC-RES-058): trigger, the provider stops its detection solution without replacement; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: market surveillance authorities, 'where necessary'; what happens with the result: not stated. No passage gives overseers access to logs, prompts, configuration, model versions or records of human review of outputs.

quotes.quote: including, where appropriate and subject to security safeguards, through application programming interfaces (API) or other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access.
Where necessary for their mandate, those national public authorities or bodies should also have access to any documentation created under this Regulation.

quotes.location: Art. 1(34)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 77(1a); p. 33
quotes.quote: the market surveillance authority shall grant the relevant public authority or body referred to in paragraph 1 access to such information or documentation, including by requesting such information or documentation from the provider or the deployer
providing transparency of the functioning of the AI system, and information about the types of data and data sources

themes.theme: Template for the public summary of training content
themes.definition: The AI Office template, with instructions, that providers of general-purpose AI models must use for the public summary of the content used to train their models.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models to publish a summary of training content 'according to a template provided by the AI Office' (Art. 53(1)(d)), and the recital says the template should be simple and effective and allow a summary in narrative form (Recital 107). The Explanatory Notice and Template (EU090) is that resource: it aims to help providers comply 'in a simple, consistent and effective manner', and the coder note says each section carries short instructions. EU088, which deals with the obligations of general-purpose AI model providers, adds that the template specifies when the summary must be updated. The four passages describe one official resource at different stages, from the legislative promise to the issued template. The duty to publish sits with model providers; public bodies figure only as possible users of such models [inference].
themes.holders: The AI Office (provides the template); providers of general-purpose AI models (use it).
themes.binding: Use of the template is statutory: the summary must be made 'according to' it (Art. 53(1)(d)). The recital says 'appropriate' and 'should'. The template itself is a provided resource. What follows from a missing or deficient summary is not stated here.

quotes.quote: It is appropriate for the AI Office to provide a template for the summary, which should be simple, effective, and allow the provider to provide the required summary in narrative form.

This Explanatory Notice and the Template annexed to it aim to help providers of general-purpose AI models comply with their obligation under Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act in a simple, consistent and effective manner.
The template that has been prepared by the AI Office specifies circumstances under which the summary must be updated.

themes.theme: Templates, forms and formats for reporting, documentation and attestation
themes.definition: Official forms, templates and documentation formats provided, promised or expected for reporting to authorities, for technical documentation and for security attestation.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act obliges the Commission to give Member States and national market surveillance and data protection authorities a template for their annual reports, including the number of decisions taken by competent judicial authorities (Art. 5(6)); the coder note says it covers the number and result of authorisation decisions. The Commission guidelines (EU043, para 419), however, say 'This template will be established in due time', so when that document was written the template required by law had not been provided. The Omnibus amendments require the Commission to establish a simplified technical documentation form for SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps; the coder note says using it is optional, but those who opt for the simplified route must use the form. The EDPS orientations on generative AI do not supply a template but say it is 'important' that EU institutions adopt and implement technical documentation models themselves, which the coder links to traceability and auditability. ENISA proposes machine-processable security attestations and software bills of materials (SBOMs) to put the 'CRA security requirements' into practice; the coder records that this is not specific to AI and that its adoption is not recorded.
themes.holders: The Commission (report template, SME form); Member States and national market surveillance and data protection authorities (users of the report template); SMEs, start-ups and SMCs (users of the form); EU institutions (expected to adopt their own documentation models); ENISA (proposer of attestation formats).
themes.binding: Statutory 'shall provide' and 'shall establish' on the Commission; the SME form is optional to adopt; the EDPS line is a recommendation ('it is important'); the ENISA item is a proposal. Not met: not stated, and the guidelines' 'in due time' sets no date.

quotes.quote: the Commission shall provide Member States and national market surveillance and data protection authorities with a template, including information on the number of the decisions taken by competent judicial authorities
This template will be established in due time.

quotes.location: Art. 1(10), replacing AI Act Art. 11(1) second su…
quotes.quote: the Commission shall establish a simplified technical documentation form targeted at the needs of SMEs, including start-ups, and SMCs.
it is important that EUIs adopt and implement technical documentation models, which can be of particular importance when the models use several datasets and / or combine different data sources

themes.theme: Labels, icons and detection tools for AI-generated content
themes.definition: Tools, icons and design features provided or encouraged so that AI-generated or manipulated content can be detected and disclosed to the people who see it.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act gives the AI Office a duty to 'encourage and facilitate' Union-level codes of practice on detecting and labelling artificially generated or manipulated content (Art. 50(7)); it does not itself supply tools. The Code of Practice (EU121) supplies an EU icon, developed by the AI Office according to the coder notes, which is publicly available and free to use without attribution, in line with placement specifications (Annex 1 has three icons). Under the Code, providers of generative AI systems are 'encouraged' to offer an optional labelling function in their interfaces, online platforms and search engines are 'encouraged' to use the EU icon or an equivalent so that deployers can meet their labelling obligation (for example in upload interfaces), and a provider that withdraws a detection solution without replacement 'will' hand it to market surveillance authorities. The Commission guidelines (EU043) say visible disclosure, as a way of reducing manipulation, 'should also be enabled through design features' built in by providers, including technical means of detecting AI-generated content. EU_Art50, which deals with the Article 50 transparency obligations [inference from its ID and content], calls the transparency Code 'the only Union-wide recognised practical framework' for providers and deployers of generative AI systems. [inference] A public body that publishes AI-generated or manipulated content as a deployer depends on providers and platforms for the means to label it.
themes.holders: The AI Office (facilitates codes, developed the icons); signatory providers of generative AI systems; signatory providers of online platforms or search engines; providers (EU043); market surveillance authorities (receive discontinued detection tools); deployers and other users (apply labels).
themes.binding: Art. 50(7) is a statutory duty to facilitate codes, not to provide tools. The Code's labelling functions and icon use are 'encouraged' and optional; handing over discontinued detection tools is a 'will' commitment that binds signatories only; EU043's 'should' is non-binding interpretation. Not met: not stated.
themes.checks: Detecting AI-generated content is a check on outputs. Trigger: for regulators, the provider stopping its detection solution without replacement (EU-ACC-RES-058); otherwise not stated. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold (for example detection accuracy): not stated. Who: market surveillance authorities, 'where necessary'; deployers and other users apply labels at their own discretion (coder note on EU-ACC-RES-053). What happens with the result: content is labelled or disclosed; no further consequence is stated.

quotes.quote: The AI Office shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level to facilitate the effective implementation of the obligations regarding the detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content.

visible disclosure constitutes a mitigating measure that should also be enabled through design features embedded in the AI system provided by the provider, including technical measures enabling the detection of AI -generated and manipulated content
An EU icon following the design specifications for visual disclosure is publicly available for everyone to use freely (see Annex 1).
it will make that solution available to the competent market surveillance authorities, subject to confidentiality and security safeguards to enable them to detect , where necessary, legacy content

themes.theme: Codes of practice and other recognised routes to show compliance
themes.definition: Instruments that regulated parties can rely on to show they meet their obligations: codes of practice, harmonised standards and regulatory sandbox exit reports.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act recital says providers 'should be able to rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance', and the coder note adds that harmonised standards, once assessed as suitable, give a presumption of conformity (Recital 117). EU088 says the general-purpose AI codes of practice set out specific measures providers 'may implement' to comply with Articles 53(1) and 55(1), and, per the coder note, calls them 'a temporary tool ... until harmonised standards are developed and approved'. EU_Art50 calls the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content 'the only Union-wide recognised practical framework' for providers and deployers of generative AI systems, and the AI Act tasks the AI Office with facilitating such codes (Art. 50(7)). Separately, the competent authority running an AI regulatory sandbox 'shall' give the provider an exit report on the activities, results and learning outcomes, which the coder note says the provider may use to demonstrate compliance in conformity assessment or market surveillance (Art. 57(7)). These are routes for providers, and under Article 50 for deployers, to show compliance; they are offered, not imposed, and one document treats codes as a stopgap while another treats the transparency Code as the sole recognised framework.
themes.holders: The AI Office (facilitates codes); providers of general-purpose AI models and providers and deployers of generative AI systems (may rely on codes); competent authorities running sandboxes (issue exit reports); providers (may use them).
themes.binding: Codes are voluntary routes ('should be able to rely', 'may implement'). The exit report is a statutory duty on the competent authority ('shall also provide'). How much weight reliance on a code carries is not stated beyond 'demonstrate compliance'.
themes.checks: Sandbox exit report (EU-ACC-RES-020): trigger, the provider's exit from the sandbox; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the competent authority, which records 'the activities carried out in the sandbox and the related results'; what happens with the result: the provider may use it as evidence in conformity assessment or market surveillance (coder note). Codes of practice: n/a.

quotes.quote: Providers should be able to rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance with the obligations.
the codes of practice lay down specific measures which providers of general -purpose AI models may implement to comply with the ir obligations laid down in Articles 53(1) and 55(1) AI Act.
the only Union-wide recognised practical framework for providers and deployers of generative AI systems
The competent authority shall also provide an exit report detailing the activities carried out in the sandbox and the related results and learning outcomes.

themes.theme: Official guidance for enforcers and the regulated
themes.definition: Guidance, guidelines and opinions issued by EU bodies to help authorities enforce, and organisations meet, accountability duties.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires the Commission to develop dedicated guidance on reporting serious incidents (Art. 73(7)), which the coder note says was to be issued by 2 August 2025 and assessed regularly. The Commission guidelines (EU043) present themselves as practical guidance both for competent authorities' enforcement and for providers' and deployers' compliance. On the data-protection side, the EDPB Opinion (EU074) gives supervisory authorities 'a framework' for assessing specific cases. For EU institutions, the EDPS points to its existing guidance rather than new AI-specific material: its guidelines on controller, processor and joint controllership (which, per the coder note, EU institutions 'should therefore rely on'), and its 'Accountability on the ground' toolkit on data protection impact assessments and prior consultation, dated February 2018 in the coder note, which the EDPS AI risk document says it complements. [inference] For EU institutions using AI, the data-protection accountability resources in these passages are general tools that predate the AI documents, not tools made for AI.
themes.holders: The Commission, the EDPB and the EDPS (provide); competent authorities, supervisory authorities, providers, deployers and EU institutions (receive).
themes.binding: Producing incident-reporting guidance is a statutory duty on the Commission; the guidance, the guidelines and the Opinion are themselves non-binding; EU institutions are 'advised' to follow the EDPS guidelines. Not met: not stated.

quotes.quote: The Commission shall develop dedicated guidance to facilitate compliance with the obligations set out in paragraph 1 of this Article.

They should serve as practical guidance to assist competent authorities under the AI Act in their enforcement activities, as well as providers and deployers of AI systems in ensuring compliance with their obligations under the AI Act
This Opinion provides a framework for competent SAs to assess specific cases where (some of) the questions raised in the Request would arise.

quotes.location: PDF p.10 (printed p.9), s.3 (fn 13); repeated PDF…
quotes.quote: EUIs are advised to follow the existing EDPS Guidelines on the concepts of controller, processor and joint controllership

themes.theme: Tools and information owed by developers and suppliers for individuals' data rights
themes.definition: Tools and information that the EDPS expects AI developers, dataset providers and suppliers to create or supply so that individuals' data-protection rights can be honoured and EU institutions can inform individuals.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS document on AI risks (EDPS_AI_risk) says AI developers or training-dataset providers 'should' create data retrieval tools so that a person exercising the right of access can be given their personal data, and, per the coder note, that such tools must securely identify and retrieve individual records; it says developers or suppliers 'should' create tools to rectify or erase personal data in the training dataset. It mentions MemHunter, an academic tool that detects personal data memorised by large language models, as something that 'could be implemented'. The EDPS orientations on generative AI say developers or suppliers 'must' provide comprehensive information about processing at each stage of development (the coder note lists dataset origin and curation or tagging), so that EU institutions can meet their transparency duties to individuals. These are resources required of the supply chain, not provided by a public authority. [inference] The EU institution that answers to individuals depends on its suppliers for the means to handle access, rectification and erasure requests and to explain processing.
themes.holders: AI developers, training personal dataset providers, developers or suppliers; academic researchers (MemHunter, mentioned only); EU institutions benefit.
themes.binding: Recommendations in EDPS guidance ('should', 'could'); 'must be provided' appears in non-binding orientations. Not met: not stated.
themes.checks: MemHunter (EU-ACC-RES-044) checks a model for memorised personal data. Trigger: a data subject's request (coder note); compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: not stated ('could be implemented'); what happens with the result: helps identify personal data for access, rectification or erasure. The retrieval, rectification and erasure tools are not checks on outputs.

quotes.quote: Data retrieval tools should be created by the AI developers or training personal dataset providers in order to provide a data subject with their personal data when invoking their right to access.
Tools such as MemHunter (automated tool to detect LLM mem orisation) could be implemented.

quotes.location: PDF p.29 (printed p.28), s.11 Informing individua…
quotes.quote: comprehensive information - that must be provided by developers or suppliers as the case may be - about the processing activities carried out at different stages of development

themes.theme: Registers, databases and public information for outside scrutiny
themes.definition: Databases, registers and published information that let the public, researchers and others see and scrutinise AI systems and models, and the support provided to fill them.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act makes the Commission the controller of the EU database (Recital 131, which the coder note says also calls for functional specifications and an independent audit report) and requires it to give providers, prospective providers and deployers 'adequate technical and administrative support' for registration, with the database meeting accessibility requirements (Art. 71(6)). JRC143539 names algorithmic registries as tools that inform citizens about AI used by public administrations, strengthen accountability and build trust, without saying who should provide them. JRC129100, in a footnote, points to the UK's algorithmic transparency standard as an example; the resource it names is outside the EU, and the passage is a mention only. The Explanatory Notice (EU090) says the public training-content summary can let academic institutions and organisations critically evaluate a general-purpose AI model's limitations and the risks of its data. [inference] The statutory register and the support for it come from the AI Act; a register of AI used by public administrations appears only in research documents, and the one concrete example given is not an EU instrument.
themes.holders: The Commission (controller of the EU database; support for registration); providers, prospective providers and deployers (receive support); public administrations (nearest actor for registries, per coder note); UK government (the example cited); academic institutions and organisations (users of the summary).
themes.binding: Art. 71(6) is a statutory 'shall' on the Commission; Recital 131 uses 'should'; the JRC passages are recommendations or description; the EU090 passage describes a benefit. Not met: not stated.

quotes.quote: It shall make available to providers, prospective providers and deployers adequate technical and administrative support.
Tools such as algorithmic registries play an important role in informing citizens about the AI solutions used by public administrations, thereby strengthening accountability and building trust.
see, e.g., the UK transparency standard https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-standard

It can allow academic institutions and organisations to critically evaluate the implications and limitations of a particuler general-purpose AI model and the potential risks and harms associated with the data used.

themes.theme: Skills, training and awareness for supervisors and staff
themes.definition: Provisions for building the knowledge and skills of supervisory staff and of the personnel who carry out disclosure duties.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act lets the European Artificial Intelligence Board help national competent authorities and the Commission build the organisational and technical expertise the Regulation needs, including by contributing to the assessment of training needs for Member States' staff (Art. 66(j)). Art. 70(3), per the coder note on EU-ACC-RES-001, requires national authority staff to have competences including an in-depth understanding of AI technologies, data and data computing, and personal data protection. Under the Code of Practice (EU121), signatory deployers of AI systems that generate deep fakes (the holder field is cut off after this) 'will make efforts proportionate to their size, available organisational resources, and capacities' to make their personnel, including external contractors (coder note), aware of the Article 50(4) and (5) disclosure obligations. These passages set competence requirements, assess training needs and require awareness; none supplies a training programme, a curriculum or money for training.
themes.holders: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (assists); national competent authorities and the Commission (benefit); Member States (staff competences); signatory deployers under the Code (staff awareness).
themes.binding: The Board's task is a power ('may', per coder); the staff competence requirement sits in the statutory Art. 70(3); the Code commitment ('will make efforts proportionate') binds signatories only, and the coder note says compliance is monitored by market surveillance authorities with no consequence stated.

quotes.quote: assist national competent authorities and the Commission in developing the organisational and technical expertise required for the implementation of this Regulation, including by contributing to the assessment of training needs for staff of Member States

Signatories will make efforts proportionate to their size, available organisational resources, and capacities to ensure awareness of the disclosure obligations under Article 50(4) and (5) AI Act among their personnel

themes.theme: The European Court of Auditors' capacity to audit AI
themes.definition: The ECA's own commitments to equip its auditors to audit AI and to share its audit methods with other public-sector auditors.
themes.what_is_set_out: The ECA's strategy (ECA_strategy) commits the Court to equip its auditors with the knowledge and skills to audit AI, including understanding AI-related risks and controls and the technical challenges such systems present (Action 4, para 54; the two coders captured this paragraph separately as EU-ACC-RES-062 and EU-ACC-RES-063), with the goal, per the coder note, that auditors are ready to audit AI-based systems and processes. It lists standards and regulations relevant to auditing AI (Annex I; the coder notes name, among others, the AI Act, the GDPR and EU DPR, ISO/IEC 42001, 38507, 5338 and 23894, ISO/IEC TR 24027 on bias, the NIST AI RMF, and IAASB and IIA material) and keeps guidance current through AWARE, described in the coder note as a methodology hub. It also commits to share its training material, methodologies and lessons learned, and to run practical workshops for the wider community of public-sector auditors. These are self-commitments by an external auditor, not statutory requirements, and they are the only passages in this cell in which a public auditor equips itself to audit AI and offers that capacity to other public auditors.
themes.holders: The European Court of Auditors and its auditors; the wider community of public-sector auditors (receive shared material); standards bodies and organisations (Annex I).
themes.binding: Self-commitments in a strategy ('we will'); not statutory; no consequence stated if not met.
themes.checks: Audit of AI-based systems. Trigger: not stated. Compared against: the standards and regulations listed in Annex I (frameworks, not metrics). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: ECA auditors. What happens with the result: not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: we will take steps to equip auditors with the necessary knowledge and skills to audit AI. Therefore, we will enhance the skills required to understand AI-related risks and controls

quotes.location: Action 6, para 61, p. 17; Annex I, pp. 22-23
quotes.quote: Annex I lists standards and regulations that are relevant for auditing AI at the time of writing.
Updates will be reflected in AWARE, ensuring that auditors have access to the most recent guidance.

We will share our training material, methodologies, and lessons learned, and we will organise practical workshops to support the wider community of public sector auditors in navigating the challenges and opportunities presented by AI.

themes.theme: Internal roles that support a body's own accountability
themes.definition: Roles inside a controller or institution whose involvement or preparatory work underpins that body's own accountability.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPB Opinion (EU074) says that when supervisory authorities assess a controller (the coder links this to publication of the legitimate-interest balancing test, para 108), 'an element to be considered' is whether the controller involved its Data Protection Officer, where one applies. The Commission document AIatEC records, under next steps, that work proceeds 'on the basis of preparatory work by the ITCB and the CMB' (the Corporate Management Board); the coder note says this preparatory work serves the Members' report to the College. That quote is a fragment and the passage, as given, does not say what the report covers [inference: it concerns the Commission's own use of AI]. Neither passage sets a duty with a consequence: DPO involvement is a factor regulators weigh, and the boards' work is an internal arrangement.
themes.holders: Controllers and their Data Protection Officer (DPO); the ITCB and the Corporate Management Board (CMB).
themes.binding: Not a duty: DPO involvement is an element supervisory authorities consider; the AIatEC passage records internal preparatory work. Not met: not stated.

quotes.quote: an element to be considered is whether the controller has involved the DPO, where applicable.
on the basis of preparatory work by the ITCB and the CMB.

absences: Of the accountability starting codes, nothing in this cell provides resources for complaint or redress routes (no support for complainants, ombudsmen or affected people; the nearest are the EDPS data-rights tools, which suppliers are asked to build), for sign-off, or for named accountable roles beyond the DPO. Sanctions are resourced only indirectly, through the Omnibus power to reclaim enforcement costs from non-compliant operators. Of the resource starting codes, time is absent (the only date is the coder-noted deadline for the Commission's incident guidance), and money appears only as 'adequate' resources, fees and cost recovery, never as an amount. National fundamental-rights bodies get access to documentation but no stated resources of their own. Little is aimed at public bodies as accountable users of AI: deployers receive registration support and labelling tools, EU institutions are pointed to existing EDPS guidance and told to adopt their own documentation models, and the only register of AI used by public administrations appears as a research recommendation citing a UK example. One resource required by law, the Commission's template for annual reports under Art. 5(6), had not yet been provided according to EU043. On checking AI outputs, there are no tools, datasets, metrics or thresholds for accuracy, consistency or repeatability, nothing on prompts, configuration, model versions or confidence scores, nothing on which cases reach a human, and no access for overseers to logs or records of human review; evaluation resources stop at independent evaluators and benchmarks still to be developed for general-purpose AI models.
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by resources for the supervisors who enforce the AI Act against providers: outside expertise (the scientific panel, testing support structures, appointed independent experts and auditors), powers of access to documentation and systems, templates, codes of practice and guidance. Money is thin: 'adequate' resources are required for national authorities and, after the Omnibus amendments, for the AI Office, but without figures, and the Omnibus adds cost recovery from non-compliant operators and fees for Member States that use the expert panel. Much of what is listed as a resource is in fact required of private parties, such as providers' remote access for supervisors, developers' data-rights tools, suppliers' information and platforms' labelling functions, so public accountability rests partly on means that must be obtained from the supply chain [inference]. Binding force is mixed: AI Act and Omnibus articles use 'shall' for the Commission and Member States, while recitals, Commission guidelines, EDPS orientations, the Code of Practice and JRC reports use 'should', 'encouraged' or 'could', and the outside expertise is almost always a power to call on help rather than a duty to use it. The main holders are the Commission and AI Office, Member States and their market surveillance authorities; the ECA is the one body here that commits to equip its own auditors to audit AI and to share that with other public auditors. Public bodies as users of AI appear mainly as EU institutions advised by the EDPS and as deployers who may receive registration support or labelling tools. On checking AI outputs, the cell provides means to evaluate general-purpose AI models (benchmarks to be developed, independent evaluators) and to detect AI-generated content, but no passage says what outputs are compared against, gives any accuracy, consistency or repeatability measure or threshold, or mentions prompts, configuration, model versions, confidence scores or which cases reach a human.
